$$
\operatorname{cos}⁡2x={cos}^{2}⁡x-{sin}^{2}⁡x

We can rewrite the above formula as

$$
-5\operatorname{cos}⁡x=-5{cos}^{2}\,(\frac{x}{2})+5{sin}^{2}\,(\frac{x}{2}).

Hence, the area of the region is

$$
\begin{aligned}A & ={\int }_{-\pi /2}^{0}(-5{cos}^{2}\,(\frac{x}{2})+5{sin}^{2}\,(\frac{x}{2})+4x+7)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi /2}^{0}(-5\operatorname{cos}⁡x+4x+7)\,\text{d}x \\  & =(-5\operatorname{sin}⁡x+2{x}^{2}+7x)\,{|}_{-\pi /2}^{0} \\  & =[-5\operatorname{sin}⁡0+2(0)^{2}+7\cdot 0]-[-5\operatorname{sin}⁡(-\frac{\pi }{2})+2{(-\frac{\pi }{2})}^{2}+7(-\frac{\pi }{2})] \\  & =0-[5+\frac{{\pi }^{2}}{2}-\frac{7\pi }{2}] \\  & =-5-\frac{{\pi }^{2}}{2}+\frac{7\pi }{2}.\end{aligned}

$A=$
{{field-1}}
questions.worked_solution:
The area of the region is given by

$$
A={\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}(4{cos}^{2}⁡(2x)+{sin}^{2}⁡(2x))\,\text{d}x.
$$

Recall  ${cos}^{2}⁡x+{sin}^{2}⁡x=1,$ so we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}4{cos}^{2}⁡(2x)+{sin}^{2}⁡(2x) & =3{cos}^{2}⁡(2x)+({sin}^{2}⁡(2x)+{cos}^{2}⁡(2x)) \\  & =3{cos}^{2}⁡(2x)+1.\end{aligned}
$$

Here, we use the double-angle formula for cosine that involves the ${cos}^{2}⁡x$ term, given by

$$
\operatorname{cos}⁡2x=2{cos}^{2}⁡x-1.
$$

 

Rearranging, we have

$$
2{cos}^{2}⁡x=\operatorname{cos}⁡2x+1.
$$

Hence, the area of the region is

$$
\begin{aligned}A & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}(3{cos}^{2}⁡(2x)+1)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}(\frac{3}{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡4x+\frac{3}{2}+1)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}(\frac{3}{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡4x+\frac{5}{2})\,\text{d}x \\  & ={(\frac{3}{8}\operatorname{sin}⁡4x+\frac{5}{2}x)|}_{0}^{\pi /4} \\  & =[\frac{3}{8}\operatorname{sin}⁡(4\cdot \frac{\pi }{4})+\frac{5}{2}\cdot \frac{\pi }{4}]-[\frac{3}{8}\operatorname{sin}⁡(4\cdot 0)+\frac{5}{2}\cdot 0] \\  & =[\frac{3}{8}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi )+\frac{5\pi }{8}]-[\frac{3}{8}\operatorname{sin}⁡(0)+0] \\  & =[\frac{3}{8}\cdot 0+\frac{5\pi }{8}]-[\frac{3}{8}\cdot 0+0] \\  & =\frac{5\pi }{8}.\end{aligned}
$$

$$

Let's recall the double-angle formula for cosine that involves the ${sin}^{2}$ term: 

$$
\operatorname{cos}⁡2\theta =1-2{sin}^{2}⁡\theta 
$$

$$
\frac{1}{2}(1-\operatorname{cos}⁡2\theta )={sin}^{2}⁡\theta .
$$

Letting $\theta =3x,$ we have

$$
\frac{1}{2}(1-\operatorname{cos}⁡(6x))={sin}^{2}⁡(3x).
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{\pi /3}^{5\pi /3}(1-5{sin}^{2}⁡(3x))\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{\pi /3}^{5\pi /3}(1-5\cdot \frac{1}{2}(1-\operatorname{cos}⁡(6x)))\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /3}^{5\pi /3}(\frac{5}{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(6x)-\frac{3}{2})\,\text{d}x \\  & ={(\frac{5}{12}\operatorname{sin}⁡(6x)-\frac{3}{2}x)\,|}_{\pi /3}^{5\pi /3} \\  & =[\frac{5}{12}\operatorname{sin}⁡(6\cdot \frac{5\pi }{3})-\frac{3}{2}\cdot \frac{5\pi }{3}]-[\frac{5}{12}\operatorname{sin}⁡(6\cdot \frac{\pi }{3})-\frac{3}{2}\cdot \frac{\pi }{3}] \\  & =[0-\frac{5\pi }{2}]-[0-\frac{\pi }{2}] \\  & =-2\pi \end{aligned}
$$

Example: 
                    Integrating Expressions Using the Double-Angle Formula for Sine
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
In this case, we use the double-angle formula for sine:

$$
\sin {2\theta} =2\sin \theta \cos \theta\quad\Rightarrow\quad \dfrac{1}{2}\sin(2\theta) = \sin{\theta}\cos{\theta}.
$$

 

Letting $\theta= \dfrac{x}{2},$ we get

$$
\eqalign{
\dfrac{1}{2} \sin \left(2\cdot \dfrac{x}{2} \right) &= \sin \left(\dfrac{x}{2} \right)\cos\left( \dfrac{x}{2}\right)\[5pt]
\dfrac{1}{2}\sin x	&= \sin \left( \dfrac{x}{2}\right) \cos  \left(\dfrac{x}{2}\right).
  }
$$

 

Therefore, 

$$
\eqalign{
		\int \sin \left(\dfrac{x}{2}\right) \cos \left(\dfrac{x}{2}\right) \, \textrm{d}x&=\int \dfrac{1}{2}\sin {x} \, \textrm{d}x\[5pt]
								&=\dfrac{1}{2} \int \sin {x} \, \textrm{d}x\[5pt]
								&=\dfrac{1}{2} \left( - \cos {x}\right )+C \[5pt]
								&=-\dfrac{1}{2} \cos {x}+C.	
	}
$$

canonical_examples.worked_solution:
We can use the double-angle formula for cosine:

$$
\cos^2\theta -\sin^2\theta=\cos 2\theta.
$$

Letting $\theta = 3x$ gives

$$
\cos^2 3x - \sin^2 3x = \cos 6x,
$$

and therefore,

$$
\eqalign{
		{\int} \left(\cos^2 3x - \sin^2 3x\right ) \, \textrm{d}x&=\int  \cos 6x\, \textrm{d}x\
								&=\dfrac{1}{6}\sin6x+ C.\
                                                                
	}
$$

canonical_examples.name:
Example: 
                    Integrating Using the Squared Cosine Variant of the Cosine Double-Angle Formula
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Here, we use the double-angle formula for cosine that involves the $\cos^2{x}$ term, given by

$$
\cos{2x} =2\cos^2 x -1.
$$

 

Rearranging, we have

$$
\cos^2 x = \dfrac{1}{2} \left(\cos 2x +1 \right).
$$

Substituting this into our integral, we get

$$
\eqalign{
		\int \cos^2 x \, \textrm{d}x&=\int  \dfrac{1}{2} \left(\cos 2x +1 \right) \, \textrm{d}x\[5pt]
								&=\dfrac{1}{2}\int ( \cos {2x} +1) \textrm{d}x\[5pt]
                                                                 &= \dfrac{1}{2}\left(\dfrac{1}{2}\sin {2x} +x\right) + C\[5pt]
								&= \dfrac{1}{4}\sin {2x} +\dfrac{1}{2}x + C.
								
	}
$$

canonical_examples.name:
Example: 
                    Integrating Using the Squared Sine Variant of the Cosine Double-Angle Formula
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Let's recall the double-angle formula for cosine that involves the $\sin^2$ term: 

$$
\cos {2\theta}=1-2\sin^2\theta.
$$

We can rearrange the above formula as

$$
\dfrac{1}{2}\left(1-\cos {2\theta} \right )=\sin^2\theta.
$$

Letting $\theta = 3x$, we have

$$
\dfrac{1}{2}\left(1-\cos {6x} \right )=\sin^2(3x).
$$

We can now integrate as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int {sin}^{2}⁡(3x)\,\text{d}x & =\int \frac{1}{2}(1-\operatorname{cos}⁡6x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\int (1-\operatorname{cos}⁡6x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(x-\frac{1}{6}\operatorname{sin}⁡6x)+C \\  & =\frac{1}{2}x-\frac{1}{12}\operatorname{sin}⁡6x+C.\end{aligned}
$$

tutorials.name: Introduction
tutorials.problem:
How can we calculate $\displaystyle{\int} \sin x \cos x \, \textrm{d}x?$  

Notice that we have the product of sine and cosine with the same argument $(x).$ In such cases, we can use the double-angle formula for sine to solve the integral.

Let's recall the double-angle formula for sine, which is

$$
\sin {2x}=2\sin x \cos x.
$$

We can rearrange the above formula as

$$
\sin x \cos x =  \dfrac{1}{2} \sin {2x}.
$$

Plugging this into our integral, we get

$$
\eqalign{
		\int \sin x \cos x \, \textrm{d}x&=\int \dfrac{1}{2}\sin {2x} \, \textrm{d}x\[5pt]
								&=\dfrac{1}{2} \int \sin {2x} \, \textrm{d}x\[5pt]
								&=\dfrac{1}{2} \left( -\dfrac{1}{2} \cos {2x}\right )+C \[5pt]
								&=-\dfrac{1}{4} \cos {2x}+C.	
	}
$$

In general, we can use the double-angle formula for sine to solve any integral that's of the form 

$$
\int \sin\left(ax+b\right)\cos(ax+b)\,\textrm{d}x.
$$

 Let's take a look at another example.
